body_markdown:
There I was, banking through the curve of a divided-highway with the 860 GT’s speedometer reading somewhere near the legal limit, when a twitch of the handlebars announced the start of a gentle weave.


The bike settled down again when I slowed slightly, but even so… Back in the[mid-1970s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/half-a-lifetime-with-a-ducati-750-imola-and-why-i-decided-to-sell-it/) , when this bike was released, Ducati’s reputation for high-speed handling and stability was second to none.


My first thought was that the GT’s tendency to get slightly lightheaded at speed was due to this particular bike’s age and condition. But a look through some old magazine tests revealed that I shouldn’t have been surprised, because[the 860 GT](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ducati/860_gt/1974/1974-ducati-860_gt-base?id=aCn1I000000DIVaSAO) was criticized for exactly the same thing when it was new in 1975.


Roland Brown


The tester from *Motorcycle Mechanics* found that the GT got “a bit upset” by a gusting cross-wind on a dual-carriageway, and that “at 90 mph it would, if something provoked it, go into a long series of weaves, not violent enough to be frightening but there all the same.”


*Bike* magazine’s tester was “sure that it’s the bike’s wide bars which lead to a slight high-speed weave over rippled surfaces.” In normal riding it never got worrying, he wrote, but when crouched over the tank at 90 mph-plus on the test strip, his left hand gripping the fork leg in U.S. flat-track-racer style to cheat the wind, the Ducati “broke into a serious yawing motion.”


*Motorcyclist* magazine’s tester, Jody Nicholas, himself a former top dirt-track racer, was generally positive about the Ducati’s handling. But he noted that the rear shock units lacked rebound damping and said that “the machine tends to wallow somewhat when cornering hard over bumpy surfaces.”


Roland Brown


Words like “weave,” “yawing,” and “wallow” had not been necessary when testing previous Ducatis, such as the 750GT, this bike’s predecessor, or the lean and racy 750 Super Sport. But they were used about the 860 by testers who were even more surprised than I was all these years later.


To be fair to the GT, not all the contemporary reviews mentioned instability; in fact, several lavished praise and regarded its handling as among the bike’s best attributes. And the issue was relatively easy to sort, because it did seem to be caused by the high, wide handlebars, which generated disruptive steering forces that even the Ducati’s basically sound chassis could not always control.


The high bars were also controversial because the resultant upright, wind-blown riding position inevitably hindered the 860’s high-speed cruising potential and gave a laid-back image that contrasted with those of previous Ducatis.


Roland Brown


Roland Brown


Roland Brown


Roland Brown


As the 860’s GT designation made clear, there was a good reason for that, in the era before fairings became standard fitment even on touring models. Ducati was attempting to broaden its reputation as a pure sporting brand, with the lucrative U.S. market particularly in mind.


The 860’s look was the work of none other than Giorgetto Giugiaro, already an auto industry star. His Italdesign house had recently created the Maserati Bora and first VW Golf, much praised for its sharp “origami” shape, and he was already working on the even more angular Lotus Esprit, due for launch in 1976.


Giugiaro gave similarly hard-edged shapes to the Ducati, his first major motorcycle project, along with Suzuki’s RE-5 rotary. The 860’s fuel tank and long, slim side panels contributed to a striking machine that was an obvious departure from the soft curves of the 750GT and Super Sport.


Response from the motorcycling press was varied. In the States, *Cycle World* enthused: “Enter the 860 GT, a Grand Touring bike. One that is built for the masses. One that is built to go fast … and will propel rider and passenger down the road in comfort. It is a far cry from previous models and opens up a new dimension for Ducati.”


Roland Brown


But *Motorcyclist* ’s Nicholas was scathing of the styling: “A couple of magazine staff like the approach taken by Mr. Giugiaro, and many current Italian automobiles are following the same design ideas. But the sharp corners, assorted angularities, and stark, bold lines impart a largeness (chunkiness?) to the motorcycle that it doesn’t deserve. Those of us who were weaned on motorcycles that followed another design philosophy are chagrined beyond words.”


The concept of a naked touring Ducati caused confusion in the U.K., where *Bike* ’s tester suggested the GT suffered from an identity crisis. “Here we have a machine that is potentially among the very best of high speed, *gran turismo* , long-distance motorcycles. Yet it doesn’t appear to know what it is, or what market segment it is expected to fill.”


Either way, the 860 GT’s bold design did at least generate plenty of attention. Ducati’s largest-capacity roadster yet also promised plenty of performance, at a significantly lower price ($2549) than that of the rarer,[racier 900 Super Sport](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorcycles/ducatis-900-super-sport-was-the-superbike-of-the-70s/) ($4300) that would follow it into showrooms a few months later.


The 860 GT, with its high handlebars, two-passenger seat, and simpler body work, lacked the racy pretensions of the 900 SS (above).


Roland Brown


The GT’s air-cooled, 864cc V-twin motor was essentially a pair of Ducati’s 450 single-cylinder motors on a common crankcase. Cylinder angle was the firm’s by-now familiar 90 degrees, with drive to the single overhead camshafts by bevel gear. The GT used conventional valve springs rather than chief engineer Fabio Taglioni’s desmodromic system, as deployed for the Super Sport models.


Ducati revealed that peak power was produced at 6900 rpm. The factory didn’t quote the output, but the tuned Super Sport produced a claimed 79 horsepower, so the GT’s figure would have been a little under 70 hp at the crankshaft.


Roland Brown


This softly tuned motor might not have had the desmo valve gear or high-revving horsepower of the SS, but by mid-1970s standards it was still an impressive powerplant. “As anyone who has done so will tell you, the only thing that beats riding a good 450 MkIII single is riding two,” one reviewer gushed. “The 860 engine has all the single’s virtues of endless torque, mechanical refinement, and sheer force of character—squared. The 860 motor is undoubtedly one of the world’s finest motorcycle engines.”


Beneath its bold blue bodywork, the Ducati’s chassis was a typical Bolognese blend of tubular steel frame and firm, Italian-made forks and shocks, supplied by Ceriani and Marzocchi, respectively. My tester bike was in good condition, especially considering Ducati’s reputation for mediocre finish. It was also standard, apart from its instruments and seat, which were from the following year’s 860 GTS.


The later seat was slightly thinner, to reduce the GT’s lofty seat height slightly. That didn’t stop the bike feeling tall when I climbed aboard, quickly becoming conscious not just of the pulled-back bars but also the forward-set footrests.


Roland Brown


Roland Brown


Roland Brown


Roland Brown


The right footpeg made itself felt almost immediately. Because this GT was lacking the electric starter that had been available as an optional extra, I had to kick-start it. I soon discovered that the footrest was perfectly placed to come into contact with a kick-starting leg, and it took a lump out of my shin—just as several testers, and doubtless customers, had experienced decades earlier.


Such inconveniences were forgiven when the big V-twin lump burst into life with a fairly restrained rumble and then proceeded to show just why it was such a good device for a sports tourer. Thanks partly to its low state of tune, the engine was superbly responsive through the mid-range.


This bike’s pair of conventionally filtered 32-mm Dell’Orto carbs looked ordinary compared to the gaping 40-mm units of the 900 Super Sport, but when tugged open they sent the bike surging forward with plenty of urgency. Like many other big Ducatis,[the V-twin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorcycles/50-years-ago-ducatis-distinctive-v-twin-birthed-a-dynasty/) was snatchy below about 3000 rpm, but it smoothed out from then on.


Vibration wasn’t a problem, even up near the 7000-rpm redline, although the big lump felt best between 3500 rpm and about 6000 rpm, and its mid-range torque meant there was little incentive to use all the revs. Generally, it was much better to change up early through the five-speed gearbox, which shifted smoothly enough to make me forgive the neutral light’s occasional duplicity.


Roland Brown


Given the slightest opportunity, the Ducati accelerated pretty rapidly toward an indicated 90 mph, though it began to feel slightly unsteady by that speed even in a straight line. It would have gone on to a maximum of about 115 mph. Those high bars meant you’d have to be both brave and strong-necked to hold high speeds for long, though, and even my steady cruising speed of a little over 70 mph became tiring after a few miles.


That noted slight high-speed weave gave Ducati’s reputation for unbeatable stability a knock but never threatened to get bad enough to cause a problem. And the bike regained some points with its handling in slower bends.


The GT’s rigid chassis and high-quality suspension gave cornering power that few bikes could match in 1975. Chassis geometry was chosen for stability, and the good thing about the wide bars was that their leverage made for easy steering.


Roland Brown


Roland Brown


Once into a turn the 860 sailed round in style, its firm suspension letting the rider know just what was going on. Only the incongruous tire choice—surely a classic Ducati should wear Pirelli Phantoms, not the Taiwanese Cheng Shins this one was equipped with—prevented me from doing the footrests more damage in the corners.


In a way, the subject of ground clearance helps explain the 860 GT’s differing reception on either side of the Atlantic. *Cycle World* ’s review enthused that: “As if you were on a racer, nothing drags when you bend the twin into a curve. And there isn’t the slightest hint of a wiggle.”


British magazine *Motorcycle Mechanics’* tester John Robinson, on the other hand, headed for the test track, where he rode sufficiently hard to drag both footrests and, over one bump, the rear brake lever, “which lifted the machine enough to cause a minor slide.” If that sounds like a flaw, Robinson then changed his line to avoid the bump, “which solved the problem and the Ducati whistled round faster than any other stock roadster we’ve tried.”


Opinions on the 860’s braking performance were also varied, with some testers praising the bike’s stopping ability but others bemoaning the single 280-mm Brembo front disc’s wooden feel at the lever. I’m in the second camp, on the evidence of this elderly bike. At least this meant I didn’t need to worry about the front tire’s lack of grip. A second disc was available as an optional extra and would have been well worth paying for.


Roland Brown


Ducati did at least demonstrate a willingness to listen to criticism. The following year the firm launched the 860 GTS, featuring not just the GT’s optional second front disc and electric starter as standard, but also flatter handlebars and a subtly reshaped fuel tank that gave it a softer look.


For European riders, the GTS was basically the Gran Turismo machine that the GT should have been all along. It started effortlessly and was well braked. And its high-speed stability was impeccable, confirming that the GT’s problem came from its bars and wind-blown riding position.


Being a Ducati, it still had a few annoying faults, particularly the corrosion-prone paint finish and switchgear that made it easy to plunge yourself into darkness when trying to operate the headlight’s dipswitch. But with a sportier riding position, the performance could be more easily used, and the essential quality of the original 860’s engine and chassis shone through.


Half a century later, Giugiaro’s striking angular lines have aged well, making Ducati’s first 864cc V-twin stand out among its ’70s stablemates. The 860 GT had its issues but fully deserves a place in the Bologna hall of fame.


Roland Brown
